report.source_text: Postoperative fundus examination of the RE was within normal limits (Fig. 1). At the same time, LE Fundus examination showed one large approximately half-a-disc diameter white, fluffy lesion with overlying retinal hemorrhages and a few scattered necrotic spots along the inferotemporal arcade. Mild optic disc pallor was noted with a macular star about 2DD away from the optic disc, the rest of the fundus was normal (Fig. 2). A slit lamp examination showed grade 1 optic disc edema. OCT showed hyperreflective signals at the level of the outer plexiform layer representing retinal exudate (Fig. 3, 4).

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 40-year-old immunocompetent man (CD4 950 cells/mm³, HIV negative) sustained right eye trauma 5 months prior to presentation. He presented with hand movement vision in the right eye and 6/60 vision in the left eye. Right eye examination revealed traumatic cataract, which was surgically removed with normal postoperative fundus examination. Left eye fundoscopy revealed classic CMV retinitis findings: a large white fluffy lesion with overlying retinal hemorrhages, necrotic spots along the inferotemporal arcade, optic disc pallor with grade 1 edema, and a characteristic macular star approximately 2 disc diameters from the optic disc. OCT imaging confirmed hyperreflective exudates at the outer plexiform layer. Serological workup showed elevated CMV IgG (1073 AU/ml) with normal CMV IgM, confirming prior CMV exposure in an immunocompetent host (normal CD4 count 950 cells/mm³, negative HIV antibody). Initial treatment with prednisolone 60 mg/day and Septran DS twice daily showed no improvement. Valganciclovir was then initiated with a loading dose of 900 mg daily for 21 days followed by maintenance therapy of 450 mg daily for 6 weeks, concurrent with prednisolone taper. At 1.5 months post-treatment initiation, left eye vision improved to 6/6 with fundoscopic evidence of healing choroiditis patch, resolving hemorrhages, and resolving macular star. Right eye fundus remained normal throughout the clinical course.
